analysis.one_liner: Taxes coal, oil, and gas at $59 per ton of carbon dioxide and spends the revenue on infrastructure and household rebates.
analysis.headline: The bill was sent to eight House committees, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would place a charge on coal, petroleum, and natural gas based on their carbon dioxide content, starting at $59 per ton and rising each year. The money would go into a trust fund for roads, transit, rail, water systems, broadband, schools, and housing, with dedicated amounts for workers and towns dependent on coal, monthly cash payments to low-income households, and a refundable tax credit for working families. It would also charge a fee on carbon-heavy imports to keep foreign producers from undercutting American ones.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income households, who would receive monthly energy refunds sized to offset the price increases the tax causes; working families, who would receive a refundable tax credit that phases out only above 350% of the poverty line; coal miners and fossil-fuel-dependent communities, who would get $7 billion a year for pensions, health benefits, retraining, and mine reclamation; and everyone who uses highways, transit, passenger rail, water systems, or broadband, which would receive dedicated multi-year funding.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-income households, coal communities, and transit users

how_it_helps.text: Creates an Energy Refund Program paying eligible households monthly cash to cover the estimated loss in purchasing power from the carbon tax, targeting households at or below 150% of the poverty line and those on SNAP, SSI, or Medicare low-income subsidies.
Creates a refundable 'working families relief' tax credit that phases out only above 350% of the poverty line, so middle-income families also recover the tax they pay through higher prices.
Dedicates $7 billion a year to workers and communities reliant on carbon-intensive industries, including pension and health benefits, workforce development, and abandoned mine reclamation.

Routes all tax revenue into a Build America Trust Fund with specified annual amounts for highways and transit, aviation, passenger rail, harbors, clean water, rural water systems, broadband, school infrastructure, public housing, and energy research.

Imposes a carbon equivalency fee on carbon-intensive imports and refunds the tax on exports, so domestic steel, cement, aluminum, glass, and chemical producers are not undercut by countries without comparable carbon pricing.

analysis.who_pays: Producers and importers of coal, petroleum, and natural gas would owe the tax, which they would pass through to consumers in the price of gasoline, heating fuel, and electricity. Households earning above the rebate thresholds would bear net higher energy costs. Manufacturers of energy-intensive goods would face higher input costs, cushioned by border adjustments.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal, oil, and gas producers and energy consumers

drawbacks.text: The tax would raise the price of gasoline, heating fuel, and electricity for every household and business, and the rebates would fully offset it only for households at or below 150% of the poverty line, leaving many working and middle-income households paying more net of the tax credit.

The tax rate is set to rise faster than ordinary inflation — the bill adjusts the $59 rate using a consumer price index increased by 6 percentage points — so the cost grows well beyond the initial rate over time.

The bill includes a deficit-neutrality provision requiring pro-rata cuts to the low-income energy refunds if trust-fund receipts fall short of what the refund program needs, so the protection for the poorest households is not guaranteed.
The border adjustment requires regulators to calculate fees and refunds on imports and exports of manufactured goods, an administratively complex system that could be contested and litigated.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a carbon tax deliberately built around protecting the people the tax would hit hardest: monthly refunds for the poorest households, a broad tax credit for working families, and dedicated aid for coal communities. The genuine cost falls on everyone who buys energy, and middle-income households above the credit phase-out would come out behind. Whether the trade is worth it depends on how one weighs steady infrastructure funding and lower emissions against higher energy prices and a fast-growing tax rate; the design answers the fairness objection that carbon taxes usually face, but not the price objection.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to eight House committees the day it was introduced, none of them ever acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended without ever reaching the House floor.

narrative.text: Rep. John Larson of Connecticut introduced the bill on May 18, 2021, joined by Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton and Rep. Stephen Lynch.
The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee and seven other committees the same day, and several subcommittees received portions of it the following day.
No committee scheduled a hearing or markup, and the bill received no further action of any kind after those referrals in May 2021.
It had only two cosponsors and died at the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023, without a floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers and importers avoided a $59-per-ton tax on their products, and households that buy energy avoided the price increases the tax would have caused; no one gained the infrastructure and rebate benefits the bill offered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers, and energy consumers

sides.party_line_note: Only three House Democrats sponsored or cosponsored the bill and no chamber ever voted on it, so no party position was ever tested on the floor.

industries.industry: Coal, oil, and natural gas producers and importers
industries.note: They would owe $59 per ton of the carbon dioxide content of what they sell, with the rate rising each year. The bill's entire funding stream comes out of their products.

industries.industry: Energy-intensive manufacturers (steel, cement, aluminum, glass, chemicals, paper)
industries.note: They would pay more for energy inputs, but the bill's border fees on carbon-intensive imports and export refunds are designed to shield them from foreign competition, and infrastructure spending would improve their freight networks.
The bill would route tens of billions a year into highways, transit, rail, harbors, water systems, broadband, schools, and housing, creating a decade of public-works contracts.
The tax would hit them at the source on the fuels they buy; they would pass the cost on to customers as higher rates, with low-income customers partly sheltered by the refund program.
